topic: General privileges: bands, emissions and power

notes.front: What is the General Class licence?
notes.back: An amateur operator licence class ranking above Technician and below Amateur Extra, granted after passing Elements 2 and 3.
notes.explanation: This topic is about exactly what a General Class control operator may and may not do on HF, compared with Technician and Extra.
notes.example: Like a driving licence tier that unlocks more roads than a learner's permit, but not every road an advanced licence allows.

notes.front: What is the Amateur Extra Class licence?
notes.back: The licence class with the widest HF privileges, with access to segments General class licensees cannot use.
notes.explanation: Several HF bands set aside narrow segments for Extra class operators only; General cards must show where those gaps fall.
notes.example: Like the top tier of a membership scheme that unlocks a few extra rooms not open to the tier below it.

notes.front: What is the Advanced Class licence?
notes.back: A licence class between General and Amateur Extra, no longer issued to new applicants but still held by some operators.
notes.explanation: 97.501 lists exam routes only to Technician, General and Amateur Extra, so no new Advanced licences are issued; Part 97 still lists its frequency privileges.
notes.example: Like a discontinued membership tier that existing members can keep, even though no new members can join it.

notes.front: What frequency range is MF (medium frequency)?
notes.explanation: The General 160 m band (1800-2000 kHz) falls inside this MF range, distinct from the HF bands above 3 MHz.
notes.example: Like a named lane on a motorway sitting between two other named lanes, each with its own defined width.

notes.front: What is an image emission?
notes.back: Facsimile and television emissions.
notes.explanation: The rules list image alongside phone as an emission type that is banned on 30 m, unlike RTTY and data.
notes.example: Like a fax machine or TV picture sent over the air, rather than voice or typed text.

notes.front: What is a data emission?
notes.back: Telemetry, telecommand and computer communications emissions, using an authorised digital code.
notes.explanation: Data is the emission type 30 m is reserved for, alongside RTTY, with no phone or image allowed there.
notes.example: Like a stream of computer-to-computer messages, as opposed to a human voice or a picture.

notes.front: What is a primary service, in frequency-sharing terms?
notes.back: A service with first claim on a shared band: secondary stations must not cause it harmful interference and must accept interference from it.
notes.explanation: Some amateur bands are shared this way with other, primary services, which is why amateurs there are the secondary user.
notes.example: Like a guest at someone else's house: the guest must not disturb the household and must put up with the household's normal noise.

notes.front: What is ERP (effective radiated power)?
notes.back: The transmitter power supplied to the antenna, multiplied by the antenna's gain relative to a half-wave dipole.
notes.explanation: The 60 m band's power limits are set in ERP, not PEP, because they depend on the antenna used as well as the transmitter.
notes.example: Like judging a torch's real brightness at a target by both its bulb wattage and how tightly its reflector focuses the beam.

notes.front: What is a 60-meter channel?
notes.back: One of four fixed centre frequencies (5332, 5348, 5373, 5405 kHz) for 60 m, alongside the 5351.5-5366.5 kHz band.
notes.explanation: These four channels exist alongside the tunable 60 m band segment, each with its own carrier offset rule and 100 W ERP limit.
notes.example: Like four fixed meeting points added alongside a whole street where you are otherwise free to stand anywhere.

notes.front: What is a digital protocol, in the rules' sense?
notes.back: A technique for RTTY or data emissions, such as CLOVER, G-TOR or PACTOR, whose technical characteristics have been documented publicly.
notes.explanation: Public documentation is the rule's condition for using a new protocol on the air, so anyone can understand what a station is transmitting.
notes.example: Like publishing the rules of a new board game before anyone is expected to play it competitively.

notes.front: On which HF bands does a General class control operator have full-band privileges, and on which are there Extra-only gaps?
notes.back: Full band: 160, 60, 30, 17, 12 and 10 m. Gaps exist on 80/75, 40, 20 and 15 m.
notes.explanation: The Extra-only gaps sit inside four bands where General privileges cover only part of the allocation.

notes.front: When a General licensee cannot use the entire voice segment of a band, which portion is available?
notes.back: The upper frequency portion.
notes.explanation: On 75, 40, 20 and 15 m the General phone segment is the upper part of the phone allocation (97.301(d) with 97.305(c)); on 160, 17, 12 and 10 m General has all of it.

notes.front: What emissions and power limit apply on the whole 30 m band, for every licensee?
notes.back: RTTY and data only, no phone or image; 200 W PEP maximum.
notes.explanation: 30 m is shared with other nations' fixed service (97.303(j)); its limits apply to every amateur licence class alike.

notes.front: Where may a General control operator transmit CW on 10 m, and what part of 10 m is available for repeaters?
notes.back: CW anywhere in the band; repeaters only above 29.5 MHz.
notes.explanation: 10 m allows CW across its whole width; 97.205(b) bars repeaters from 28.0-29.5 MHz, so only 29.5-29.7 MHz is left for them.

notes.front: What must an amateur station do when the amateur service is designated secondary on a band?
notes.back: Not cause harmful interference to, and accept interference from, the primary-service stations.
notes.explanation: This is a two-way obligation: avoid causing trouble, and tolerate trouble caused by the higher-priority user.

notes.front: What is the maximum transmitter power allowed anywhere in the amateur bands, and how is it measured?
notes.back: 1500 W PEP output, measured as PEP output from the transmitter.
notes.explanation: This is the general ceiling; it is lower on specific segments such as 30 m, where 200 W PEP applies to everyone.

notes.front: What is the maximum emission bandwidth on 60 m, and what must be kept on record for a non-dipole antenna there?
notes.back: 2.8 kHz; the antenna's gain.
notes.explanation: These two limits together control both the signal's width and its effective power, given that 60 m power limits are set in ERP.

notes.front: What is the maximum ERP on the 5351.5-5366.5 kHz 60 m segment?
notes.back: 9.15 W ERP.
notes.explanation: This is far below the 100 W ERP allowed on the four fixed 60 m channels, so a station retuning from a channel to this segment must cut power.

notes.front: What must be true of a new digital protocol before it is used on the air?
notes.back: Its technical characteristics must be publicly documented.
notes.explanation: This keeps every amateur digital protocol open for anyone to understand and decode, rather than proprietary.

notes.front: On which HF and/or MF amateur bands are there portions where General class licensees cannot transmit?
notes.back: 80 meters, 40 meters, 20 meters, and 15 meters
notes.choices:
A) 60 meters, 30 meters, 17 meters, and 12 meters
B) 160 meters, 60 meters, 15 meters, and 12 meters
C) 80 meters, 40 meters, 20 meters, and 15 meters
D) 80 meters, 20 meters, 15 meters, and 10 meters
notes.choicesExplained: A: General has full privileges on 60, 30, 17 and 12 m, with no Extra-only gap. B: 160, 60 and 12 m are full-band for General; only 15 m has a gap. D: 10 m has no Extra-only segment.
notes.explanation: Each of these four bands carries a narrow segment reserved for Amateur Extra licensees, which General class control operators must avoid.

notes.front: On which of the following bands is phone operation prohibited?
notes.back: 30 meters
notes.choices:
A) 160 meters
B) 30 meters
C) 17 meters
D) 12 meters
notes.choicesExplained: A, C, D: each of these bands authorises phone operation in at least part of the band; only 30 m bans phone entirely.
notes.explanation: 30 m is limited to RTTY and data emissions for every licence class, with no phone or image allowed.

notes.front: On which of the following bands is image transmission prohibited?
notes.back: 30 meters
notes.choices:
A) 160 meters
B) 30 meters
C) 20 meters
D) 12 meters
notes.choicesExplained: A, C, D: image transmission is authorised on parts of each of these bands; only 30 m bans it entirely.
notes.explanation: Like phone, image emissions are excluded from 30 m, which is reserved for RTTY and data.

notes.front: On which of the following frequencies are General class licensees prohibited from operating as control operator?
notes.back: 7.125 MHz to 7.175 MHz
notes.choices:
A) 7.125 MHz to 7.175 MHz
B) 28.000 MHz to 28.025 MHz
C) 21.275 MHz to 21.300 MHz
D) All these choices are correct
notes.choicesExplained: B: 28.000-28.025 MHz on 10 m is within General privileges. C: 21.275-21.300 MHz on 15 m is within the General phone segment. D: only choice A is actually an Extra-only gap.
notes.explanation: This narrow segment of 40 m is reserved for Amateur Extra class control operators.

notes.front: Which of the following applies when the FCC rules designate the amateur service as a secondary user on a band?
notes.back: Amateur stations must not cause harmful interference to primary users and must accept interference from primary users
notes.choices:
A) Amateur stations must record the call sign of the primary service station before operating on a frequency assigned to that station
B) Amateur stations may use the band only during emergencies
C) Amateur stations must not cause harmful interference to primary users and must accept interference from primary users
D) Amateur stations may only operate during specific hours of the day, while primary users are permitted 24-hour use of the band
notes.choicesExplained: A: no such call-sign-recording requirement exists. B: secondary status does not restrict amateur use to emergencies only. D: there is no fixed time-of-day restriction tied to secondary status.
notes.explanation: Secondary status is a two-way obligation: avoid interfering with the primary service, and accept interference it causes.

notes.front: On which amateur frequencies in the 10-meter band may stations with a General class control operator transmit CW emissions?
notes.back: The entire band
notes.choices:
A) 28.000 MHz to 28.025 MHz only
B) 28.000 MHz to 28.300 MHz only
C) 28.025 MHz to 28.300 MHz only
D) The entire band
notes.choicesExplained: A, B, C: each restricts CW to only part of 10 m, but the rule authorises CW on any frequency across the whole band.
notes.explanation: CW is authorised across the full 10 m band, unlike phone, which is limited to part of it.

notes.front: Which HF bands have segments exclusively allocated to Amateur Extra licensees?
notes.back: 80 meters, 40 meters, 20 meters, and 15 meters
notes.choices:
A) All HF bands
B) 80 meters, 40 meters, 20 meters, and 15 meters
C) All HF bands except 160 meters and 10 meters
D) 60 meters, 30 meters, 17 meters, and 12 meters
notes.choicesExplained: A: not all HF bands carry an Extra-only segment. C: this overstates how many bands have an Extra-only gap. D: General has full privileges on 60, 30, 17 and 12 m.
notes.explanation: These four bands each set aside a narrow segment that only Amateur Extra control operators may use.

notes.front: Which of the following frequencies is within the General class portion of the 15-meter band?
notes.choices:
A) 14250 kHz
B) 18155 kHz
C) 21300 kHz
D) 24900 kHz
notes.choicesExplained: A: 14250 kHz is in the 20 m band, not 15 m. B: 18155 kHz is in the 17 m band. D: 24900 kHz is in the 12 m band.
notes.explanation: 21300 kHz falls within the General phone segment of 15 m, 21.275-21.450 MHz.

notes.front: What portion of the 10-meter band is available for repeater use?
notes.back: The portion above 29.5 MHz
notes.choices:
A) The entire band
B) The portion between 28.1 MHz and 28.2 MHz
C) The portion between 28.3 MHz and 28.5 MHz
D) The portion above 29.5 MHz
notes.choicesExplained: A: repeaters are not authorised across the whole band. B, C: 97.205(b) bars repeaters below 29.5 MHz on 10 m.
notes.explanation: 97.205(b) bars 10 m repeaters from 28.0-29.5 MHz, leaving only the band above 29.5 MHz for them.

notes.front: When General class licensees are not permitted to use the entire voice portion of a band, which portion of the voice segment is available to them?
notes.back: The upper frequency portion
notes.choices:
A) The lower frequency portion
B) The upper frequency portion
C) The lower frequency portion on frequencies below 7.3 MHz, and the upper portion on frequencies above 14.150 MHz
D) The upper frequency portion on frequencies below 7.3 MHz, and the lower portion on frequencies above 14.150 MHz
notes.choicesExplained: A: the lower portion is generally reserved for Extra, not General. C, D: there is no such split rule that changes with frequency; the upper portion applies consistently.
notes.explanation: General's partial voice segments consistently sit at the top of each band's phone allocation.

notes.front: What is the maximum transmitter power an amateur station may use on 10.140 MHz?
notes.back: 200 watts PEP output
notes.choices:
A) 200 watts PEP output
B) 1000 watts PEP output
C) 1500 watts PEP output
D) 2000 watts PEP output
notes.choicesExplained: B, C, D: these exceed the 200 W PEP ceiling that applies to the whole 30 m band, for every licence class.
notes.explanation: 10.140 MHz falls in 30 m, where every licensee is limited to 200 W PEP regardless of class.

notes.front: What is the maximum transmitter power an amateur station may use on the 12-meter band?
notes.back: 1500 watts PEP output
notes.choices:
A) 50 watts PEP output
B) 200 watts PEP output
C) 1500 watts PEP output
D) An effective radiated power equivalent to 100 watts from a half-wave dipole
notes.choicesExplained: A, B: these are far below the general 1500 W PEP ceiling. D: 12 m power is limited in PEP, not ERP; that measure applies to 60 m instead.
notes.explanation: 12 m has no special lower limit, so the general 1500 W PEP ceiling applies.

notes.front: What is the maximum bandwidth permitted by FCC rules for amateur radio stations transmitting on USB frequencies in the 60-meter band?
notes.back: 2.8 kHz
notes.choices:
A) 2.8 kHz
B) 5.6 kHz
C) 1.8 kHz
D) 3 kHz
notes.choicesExplained: B: 5.6 kHz is double the actual limit. C: 1.8 kHz is narrower than the rule allows. D: the rule sets 2.8 kHz for all 60 m emissions (97.303(h)(3); 97.307(f)(14)).
notes.explanation: The rule sets 2.8 kHz as the maximum for all 60 m emissions, not just USB phone.

notes.front: Which of the following is required by the FCC rules when operating in the 60-meter band?
notes.back: If you are using an antenna other than a dipole, you must keep a record of the gain of your antenna
notes.choices:
A) If you are using an antenna other than a dipole, you must keep a record of the gain of your antenna
B) You must keep a record of the date, time, frequency, power level, and stations worked
C) You must keep a record of all third-party traffic
D) You must keep a record of the manufacturer of your equipment and the antenna used
notes.choicesExplained: B: a detailed contact log is not what 60 m rules specifically require. C: no rule requires a record of third-party traffic. D: manufacturer records are not required.
notes.explanation: Since 60 m power limits are set in ERP relative to a half-wave dipole, a non-dipole antenna's gain must be on record to show compliance.

notes.front: What is the limit for transmitter power on the 28 MHz band for a General Class control operator?
notes.back: 1500 watts PEP output
notes.choices:
A) 100 watts PEP output
B) 1000 watts PEP output
C) 1500 watts PEP output
D) 2000 watts PEP output
notes.choicesExplained: A, B: these are below the actual General ceiling on 10 m. D: 2000 W exceeds the maximum allowed anywhere in the amateur bands.
notes.explanation: 10 m (28 MHz) carries no special reduced limit for General, so the general 1500 W PEP ceiling applies.

notes.front: What is the limit for transmitter power on the 1.8 MHz band?
notes.back: 1500 watts PEP output
notes.choices:
A) 200 watts PEP output
B) 1000 watts PEP output
C) 1200 watts PEP output
D) 1500 watts PEP output
notes.choicesExplained: A: 200 W is the 30 m limit, not 160 m. B, C: neither matches the actual 1500 W PEP ceiling.
notes.explanation: 160 m (1.8 MHz) has no special reduced limit, so the general 1500 W PEP ceiling applies here too.

notes.front: What must be done before using a new digital protocol on the air?
notes.back: Publicly document the technical characteristics of the protocol
notes.choices:
A) Type-certify equipment to FCC standards
B) Obtain an experimental license from the FCC
C) Publicly document the technical characteristics of the protocol
D) Submit a rule-making proposal to the FCC describing the codes and methods of the technique
notes.choicesExplained: A: no type-certification is required for a new protocol. B: no experimental licence is required. D: no FCC rule-making submission is required.
notes.explanation: Public documentation, not any FCC filing, is the rule's condition for using a new digital protocol.

notes.front: What measurement is specified by FCC rules that regulate maximum power?
notes.back: PEP output from the transmitter
notes.choices:
A) RMS output from the transmitter
B) RMS input to the antenna
C) PEP input to the antenna
D) PEP output from the transmitter
notes.choicesExplained: A, B: power limits are set in PEP, not RMS. C: the rule specifies output from the transmitter, not input to the antenna.
notes.explanation: Most amateur power limits, including the general 1500 W ceiling, are defined as PEP output from the transmitter.

notes.front: A station runs 5 W PEP into a dipole (0 dBd gain) on 5360 kHz. Is this within the 60 m ERP limit for that segment?
notes.back: Yes; ERP equals 5 W, below the 9.15 W ERP limit for 5351.5-5366.5 kHz.
notes.explanation: With a dipole's gain of 1 (0 dBd), ERP equals PEP output, so 5 W PEP stays under the 9.15 W ceiling.

notes.front: What is the difference between the 30 m power limit and the general amateur power limit?
notes.back: 30 m is capped at 200 W PEP for every licence class; most other bands allow up to the general 1500 W PEP ceiling.
notes.explanation: 30 m is shared with other nations' fixed service (97.303(j)), unlike most other HF bands.
notes.contrast: 30 m: 200 W PEP, all classes, all the time. General ceiling: 1500 W PEP, applies where no band-specific limit is lower.

notes.front: What is the difference between a PEP power limit and an ERP power limit?
notes.back: A PEP limit is set purely by transmitter output; an ERP limit also factors in the antenna's gain relative to a half-wave dipole.
notes.explanation: 60 m's ERP limits mean a high-gain antenna must run less transmitter power than a dipole to stay within the same legal limit.
notes.contrast: PEP limit (e.g. 30 m, 1500 W ceiling): transmitter output only. ERP limit (60 m): transmitter output x antenna gain relative to a dipole.

notes.front: What is the difference in where General may operate CW versus phone on the 10 m band?
notes.back: CW is authorised across the entire 10 m band; phone is authorised only in part of the band.
notes.explanation: 97.305(a) allows CW on any frequency the control operator may use, while phone is confined to specific segments as on other HF bands.
notes.contrast: 10 m CW: entire band, any frequency. 10 m phone: only the segments authorised for phone emissions.
